In transition elements, the d orbitals are responsible for the development of colour in the transition compound. When these orbitals form bonds with the ligands, they splits up, e.g. in octahedral complexes they divide into two energy levels, one set has higher energy than the other. 14.2.4 Colour of Complexes

Most of the compounds of the transition metals are coloured in solid or solution state. In transition elements, the d orbitals are responsible for the development of colour in the transition compound. When these orbitals form bonds with the ligands, they splits up, e.g. in octahedral complexes they divide into two energy levels, one set has higher energy than the other. The electrons residing in low energy d-orbital absorb a part of the visible light and jump to higher energy d-orbital. This process is called d – d transition.

When light is allowed to fall on a substance, it absorbs from it the light of a particular colour whose wavelength is in the visible region (4000 – 7000Å) and reflects or transmits back the remaining light which is the colour complementary to that of the absorbed light. The colour of the transmitted light is different from the colour of the absorbed light and is known as the complementary colour of the absorbed light. The colour of the transition metal complex is the colour of this transmitted light.

Tidbit — Complementary Colours

Colours directly opposite each other on the colour wheel are said to be complementary colours. Blue and yellow are complementary colours; red and cyan are complementary; and so are green and magenta. Copper (II) sulphate solution is pale blue (cyan) because it absorbs light in the red region of the spectrum. Thus, cyan is the complementary colour of red.

If the complex absorbs all colours except orange, the complex appears orange. The complex will also appear orange if it absorbs only light of the colour blue. In a complementary manner, if the complex ion absorbed only orange, it would appear blue. Blue and orange are referred to as complementary colours. In [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺, yellow and green lights are absorbed, while most of the blue and red lights are transmitted, therefore the solution of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ions looks purple in colour.

رنگوں کے دائرے میں بالکل آمنے سامنے رنگ تکمیلی رنگ ہیں۔ نیلا اور پیلا، سرخ اور سیان، اور سبز اور میجنٹا تکمیلی ہیں۔ کاپر(II) سلفیٹ کا محلول ہلکا نیلا (سیان) ہے کیونکہ وہ طیف کے سرخ علاقے کی روشنی جذب کرتا ہے۔ یوں سیان سرخ کا تکمیلی رنگ ہے۔

کمپلیکس نارنجی کے سوا تمام رنگ جذب کرے تو نارنجی دکھائی دیتا ہے۔ صرف نیلی روشنی جذب کرے تو بھی نارنجی ہے۔ تکمیلی طور پر صرف نارنجی جذب کرنے والا کمپلیکس آئن نیلا دکھائی دیتا ہے۔ نیلا اور نارنجی تکمیلی رنگ ہیں۔ [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ میں پیلی اور سبز روشنی جذب جبکہ بیشتر نیلی اور سرخ روشنی منتقل ہوتی ہے، اس لیے ان آئنوں کا محلول جامنی ہے۔

مکمل بھرے یا خالی d آربیٹل والے آئن بے رنگ ہیں، مثلاً Cu⁺(3d¹⁰)، Zn²⁺(3d¹⁰)، Sc³⁺(3d⁰) اور Ti⁴⁺(3d⁰) کے کمپلیکس بے رنگ ہیں۔

14.2.4 Colour of Complexes

Most of the compounds of the transition metals are coloured in solid or solution state. In transition elements, the d orbitals are responsible for the development of colour in the transition compound. When these orbitals form bonds with the ligands, they splits up, e.g. in octahedral complexes they divide into two energy levels, one set has higher energy than the other. The electrons residing in low energy d-orbital absorb a part of the visible light and jump to higher energy d-orbital. This process is called d – d transition.

When light is allowed to fall on a substance, it absorbs from it the light of a particular colour whose wavelength is in the visible region (4000 – 7000Å) and reflects or transmits back the remaining light which is the colour complementary to that of the absorbed light. The colour of the transmitted light is different from the colour of the absorbed light and is known as the complementary colour of the absorbed light. The colour of the transition metal complex is the colour of this transmitted light.

Tidbit — Complementary Colours

Colours directly opposite each other on the colour wheel are said to be complementary colours. Blue and yellow are complementary colours; red and cyan are complementary; and so are green and magenta. Copper (II) sulphate solution is pale blue (cyan) because it absorbs light in the red region of the spectrum. Thus, cyan is the complementary colour of red.

If the complex absorbs all colours except orange, the complex appears orange. The complex will also appear orange if it absorbs only light of the colour blue. In a complementary manner, if the complex ion absorbed only orange, it would appear blue. Blue and orange are referred to as complementary colours. In [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺, yellow and green lights are absorbed, while most of the blue and red lights are transmitted, therefore the solution of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ions looks purple in colour.
